extracted.intended_audience: political scientists, public-administration researchers, and policy analysts studying U.S. notice-and-comment rulemaking and public comment influence
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical evaluation of how public comments (especially on environmental justice) affect draft-to-final rule text and policy outcomes using logit models, text-change measures, and network/coalition analysis. Includes methodological recommendations for measuring influence and representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence matching as primary text-change measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Use sentence matching to detect whether and how agencies changed discussion of environmental justice (EJ) between draft and final rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: computationally faster, avoids section-numbering/section-matching problems, and captures EJ attention outside a formal EJ section (e.g., in the response-to-comments section). If an agency is paying attention to EJ issues, sentence matching will likely detect it. Caveats: other measures (see separate entry) could complement sentence matching for robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative text-change measures (percent sentences/words, topic proportions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complement or supplement sentence matching with other measures: percent of EJ-containing sentences changed, percent of words in a section that changed, or change in topic proportions (Judge-Lord, 2017).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These alternative measures may detect subtler shifts in emphasis or framing that sentence matching misses. Recommended as useful robustness checks or for future work to capture magnitude/extent of change rather than binary sentence edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent variable: "EJ Added" (whether EJ is added to final rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Binary outcome indicating whether an agency added explicit mentions/discussion of 'environmental justice' in the final rule when the draft rule did not address EJ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to test the Distributive Claims Hypothesis: rules are more likely to add EJ language when comments raise EJ concerns. Interpretation often presented via predicted probabilities rather than raw logit coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent variable: "EJ Changed" (whether EJ discussion changed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Binary outcome for rules that already discussed EJ in the draft: whether any sentences containing 'environmental justice' changed between draft and final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to assess responsiveness in how EJ is discussed (not just whether it appears). Interpretation should consider baseline agency tendencies (e.g., EPA had high baseline change rates) and interaction with comment volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictor: whether comments raised EJ concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicator for whether any public comments explicitly raised environmental-justice/distributive-justice concerns on a proposed rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary predictor for testing whether claims about distributive justice affect agency discourse. Analyze both presence/absence and counts (unique commenters) to distinguish signal strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictor: number of unique (non-form letter) EJ comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Count (typically logged) of distinct, non-form-letter public comments that mention environmental justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supports the Repeated Claims Hypothesis: more unique EJ comments increase the probability that EJ appears or is changed; helps distinguish genuine repeated claims from form-letter volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictor: total number of comments (including form letters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count (typically logged) of all public comments received on a rule, including form letters and mass submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to test Public Attention and Public Pressure hypotheses: overall comment volume proxies for public attention/salience. Effects may differ depending on whether the draft already includes EJ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction: EJ comment presence × total comments (EJ Comment*Log(Comments+1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Interaction term between presence (or count) of EJ comments and the overall number of comments to detect whether the effect of EJ comments varies with salience/volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings: negative interaction — as total comments increase, the marginal relationship between EJ comments and agencies addressing EJ shrinks (especially in very high-volume dockets). Use interaction plots/predicted probabilities to interpret.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model specification: logit regressions with fixed effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate binary outcomes (EJ Added, EJ Changed) via logistic regression. Include fixed effects for presidential administration and, where specified, agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models 1/3 include president fixed effects; Models 2/4 also include agency fixed effects. Including agency FE isolates within-agency variation; present predicted probabilities holding other covariates at modal values for interpretability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use predicted probabilities/plots to interpret logit results
rubrics_metrics.description: Because logit coefficients are not easily interpretable, present predicted probabilities (e.g., Figures 4.5–4.9) to show substantive effects across values of key predictors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hold other variables at modal values (author used EPA, zero additional EJ comments, one comment total or median counts) when plotting. Use these plots to show how probability of adding/changing EJ varies by president, number of comments, and agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting effects at low vs high comment volumes
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate effects of EJ comments at low numbers of total comments (typical cases) versus very high comment volumes (salient rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At low comment counts, a single EJ comment meaningfully increases probability of EJ being added (e.g., ~30% increase for <10 comments). At extremely high volumes (e.g., 10,000+ comments), presence of EJ comments often no longer has a significant marginal effect — estimate uncertainty is high because few such rules lack EJ comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Attention Hypothesis (operationalization and interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothesis that greater overall public attention (more comments) increases the probability of policy change (e.g., adding EJ language).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize via logged total comments. Findings: supports adding EJ where none existed (probability of adding increases with comment volume), but not uniformly — interaction with EJ comments matters and patterns reverse for rules that already discuss EJ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeated Claims Hypothesis (operationalization and interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothesis that repeated independent claims (more unique commenters raising EJ) increase the probability of policy change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize via number of unique EJ comments; models 2–4 show a positive relationship, supporting the hypothesis that repeated claims increase probability of EJ language being added or changed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy Receptivity Hypothesis (agency heterogeneity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions differ in norms, procedures, and internal capacity to see and act on EJ claims, so responsiveness varies by agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect agencies with dedicated EJ staff/guidance (EPA, DOT components) to have higher baseline rates of adding/changing EJ; include agency fixed effects and present agency-level predicted probabilities (Figure 4.7). Interpret differences cautiously where sample sizes of EJ-change events are small.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different relationship when draft already addresses EJ (salience/hard-to-change effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: For rules that already addressed EJ in the draft, total comment counts are inversely related to change: more comments correlate with lower probability of changing how EJ is discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: highly salient rules may reflect an agency’s anticipated final position, making them harder to change. When draft already includes EJ, specific EJ comments still have a small positive relationship with change at typical (low) comment levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine three complementary methods to assess influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Triangulate causal claims using (1) large-scale hand-coded lobbying-success measures, (2) detailed case studies/process tracing, and (3) computational methods measuring draft-to-final document change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each method addresses different threats (measurement, causal inference). Use computational text-change for broad coverage, hand-coded lobbying outcomes for actor-level influence, and case studies for causal mechanisms and temporal ordering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disaggregate dimensions of policy conflict (avoid single spatial coding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not reduce policy support/opposition to a single spatial dimension — policies often contain multiple conflict dimensions (e.g., tribal sovereignty vs environmental protection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code policies into multiple issue-dimensions and assess coalition positions per dimension to better capture who supported/opposed what; refines measures of lobbying success and coalition dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Network and coalition analysis as evaluative tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat organizations as network nodes and lobbying coalitions as edges; analyze centrality, coalition composition, and time-varying ties to understand mobilization structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use node centrality to identify dominant mobilizers; exploit timestamps and policy-linked comments to study sequence (who comments first, who amplifies). Consider platform/technology layers (Care2, VoterVoice, change.org) as additional nodes/edges shaping mobilization patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study agency processing of comments via FOIA and comment metadata
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate how agencies process public comments (consultant summaries, tags like 'Mass comment - organization unknown', how agencies fill missing commenter metadata) to infer whether agencies recognized/linked mass campaigns to organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain consultant summaries and instructions via FOIA; variation in whether agencies tag/formally associate comments with organizations may provide leverage on whether agencies are aware of organized campaigns and capable of responding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for endogeneity of mobilization decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that organizations choose to mobilize based on perceived probability of success and issue characteristics (endogeneity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure relative effort invested in sophisticated lobbying (hiring lawyers/scientists/consultants) versus mass mobilization; small sophisticated-lobbying investment but large mass mobilization may indicate motives other than affecting policy. Use such measures to partially address selection on mobilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-order representation quality as an evaluative dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess who is actually represented by mobilizing organizations and whether national organizations partner meaningfully with frontline/local groups to raise specific EJ claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine coalition composition and the presence/absence of place-based actors; evaluate whether generalized national claims ('all people' or 'low-income communities of color') differ in policy impact from specific community-rooted claims (e.g., fish-consumption risks for tribes). This affects how we evaluate democratic legitimacy of comment-driven influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting statistical significance and fit (conventional thresholds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Report p-value thresholds and model fit statistics when presenting regression tables (e.g., + p<0.1, * p<0.05, ** p<0.01, *** p<0.001; AIC/BIC/LogLik).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include model diagnostics, number of observations, and fixed effects specification. Use predicted probabilities and confidence bounds in figures to convey substantive uncertainty, especially where sample sizes are small (e.g., few rules adding EJ in many agencies).
